query: For magnetic high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could increase the coercive field? State one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to alter coercivity, the predicted outcome relative to a matched baseline, the conditions under which the effect should hold, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Short-time intermediate-temperature aging (~700°C for a few hours) of AlCoFeNi-based high-entropy alloys will induce partial B2 precipitation in the A2 matrix, raising the coercive field by at least 20% relative to as-cast or fully homogenized alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or fully homogenized AlCoFeNi-based high-entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Aging treatment at approximately 700°C for a few hours to promote B2 precipitation within the A2 matrix
generation.conditions: Applied to ferromagnetic AlCoFeNi-based alloys that form partial B2/A2 microstructures near ~700°C under standard vacuum or inert-gas heat-treatment conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Refined B2 precipitates in an A2 matrix
generation.mechanism: Newly formed nanoscale B2 regions act as additional barriers to domain wall motion, thereby increasing the coercive field
generation.predicted_outcome: A ≥20% increase in coercivity compared with the unaged baseline condition
generation.baseline: Coercive field of the as-cast or fully homogenized material before the aging step
generation.boundary: Effect may diminish at different compositions or prolonged aging that leads to excessive precipitation coarsening, thereby reducing the net gain in coercivity
generation.uncertainty: Optimal aging durations and temperatures for maximizing B2-driven pinning are not fully determined and may vary with alloy composition

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare AlCoFeNi-based HEA samples with identical initial conditions and subject one batch to 700°C aging for a few hours while leaving the control batch in as-cast or homogenized state. Compare their microstructures and magnetic hysteresis curves.
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy to confirm the presence or absence of B2 precipitates
Measurement of coercive field (Hc) via standard magnetization tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If aged samples exhibit no partial B2 precipitation and fail to show at least a 20% coercivity increase versus the unaged control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The saturation magnetization (MS) and coercivity (Hc) for the four different samples analyzed in the present study have been listed in Table 1. The MS of AlCoFeNi is substantially higher compared to that of the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy for both heat-treated conditions. While the magnetization is primarily determined by composition and the crystal structure, the coercivity can be affected by impurities, deformation, grain size and phase decomposition. The coercivity (Hc) decreased with increasing annealing temperature from 15 Oe for sample aged at 600 °C/15 h, exhibiting nanoscale phase separation, to 4 Oe for samples aged at 1000 °C/15 h, exhibiting a homogeneous undecomposed B2 matrix. A similar observation has been reported in the literature, where the coercivity of the AlCoCrCuFeNi HEA annealed at 1000 °C/2 h decreases by 30 Oe (from 45 Oe to 15 Oe) compared to as-cast alloys. The AlCoFeNi HEA investigated in the present study exhibits higher saturation magnetization and lower coercivity than other soft ferrite magnetic materials, e.g., MnZn ferrite, Cu-Zn-Ti ferrite,, as revealed in Supplementary Table 2.

cited_evidence.text: The magnetic texture in the AlCoFeNi HEA (Figure 2) is characterized by large magnetic domains with small-angle magnetization variations. Magnetic domain walls move easily in the presence of an applied magnetic field. In contrast, in the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi HEA, which has a multi-scale hierarchical B2+A2 decomposed structure, the A2 spheres in region R1 support 3D magnetic vortex states in the B2 matrix (Figure 5), with a random distribution of clockwise and anticlockwise field rotations. Based on these observations, magnetization reversal and domain wall movement across the different magnetic components are expected to be highly complex processes. Our magnetic switching study (Figure 6) shows that, in region R1, magnetic vortices in A2 gen-2 precipitates can change their rotation direction in the presence of external magnetic fields of 100–500 mT. The smaller the diameter of the A2 gen-2 precipitate, the lower is the magnetic field that is needed to change the magnetic vortex rotation direction, suggesting that the coercivity of such an AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi HEA can be tuned by changing the sizes and separations of the constituent A2 precipitates and islands. decision.trend: Early work (PMC6197204) showed that partial substitution (e.g., Co by Cr) in AlCoFeNi high-entropy alloys could increase coercivity but reduced saturation magnetization, highlighting that chemical modifications impact domain wall motion. More recently (PMC8961229), researchers uncovered the direct link between a hierarchically decomposed B2 + A2 microstructure and complex magnetic domains and vortices that control coercivity. The progression has thus involved compositional tuning, followed by recognition that microstructural refinement of B2/A2 phases may offer a pathway to systematically enhancing coercive fields.
decision.unsolved: Despite evidence that controlling microstructure (e.g., refining B2 segregation) can increase coercivity in magnetic high-entropy alloys without resorting to extensive compositional shifts, an optimized processing route for reliably raising coercivity—while preserving other key magnetic properties—remains elusive. The coupling between hierarchical phase decomposition and domain wall pinning has not been fully leveraged in a simple, single-step intervention.
decision.lever: Apply intermediate-temperature aging (e.g., ~700°C for a few hours) to promote partial B2/A2 phase decomposition and domain wall pinning.
decision.why: Testable hypothesis: A short-time aging at approximately 700°C will induce a refined B2 precipitate distribution within the A2 matrix, increasing the coercive field by at least 20% compared with the as-cast or fully homogenized baseline. The mechanism is that newly formed or refined B2 precipitates create additional magnetic domain boundaries that obstruct domain wall motion. Prior work (PMC6197204, PMC8961229) has shown how B2 phase formation and dismantling can afect coercivity. The effect should hold for AlCoFeNi-based alloys that exhibit incomplete or partial phase decomposition at this temperature. An appropriate experiment is to prepare identical samples, subject one batch to the specified aging treatment, and measure magnetic hysteresis loops. A higher measured coercivity for the aged samples would support the hypothesis; if no enhancement is measured or if B2 refinement is not observed by electron microscopy, the hypothesis would be falsified.
